idiom_name: goroutines ranged over a buffered channel, driven by the runtime network poller
implementation_notes: Go already implements the pattern inside the runtime: the netpoller is the asynchronous layer (a goroutine blocked in a socket read consumes no operating-system thread - a blocked DNS request consumes only a goroutine, as the net package documents), while ordinary goroutines are the synchronous layer that may block freely on I/O, locks and databases. The queueing layer collapses into a buffered channel and the hand-off into a channel send, so a worker pool is N goroutines ranging over one channel. Keep the explicit structure only where the pool must be bounded (a shared resource with a concurrency cap) or where the queue must be observable, durable or droppable.
pitfalls: A channel send on an unbuffered channel makes the accept loop the throughput limit; buffer the queue and decide explicitly what happens when it is full (drop, shed, block).
range over a channel ends only when the channel is closed, so a missing shutdown path parks workers forever and leaks goroutines.
Blocking calls into cgo or raw syscalls hold an operating-system thread, which breaks the cheap-blocking assumption the pattern relies on.
Sending a struct that still aliases the connection's read buffer across the channel hands ownership of memory two goroutines may touch.
